extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and policymakers interested in U.S. net neutrality policy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and evaluating legal, regulatory, and policy standards applied to net neutrality in the United States, including FCC orders, court holdings, and legislative conditions. Covers principles (e.g., transparency, no-blocking), statutory bases (Title I/II, Section 706), and policy conditions used in rulemaking and spectrum auctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to access content
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers should have access to their choice of legal content. (One of Michael Powell's four 'Preserving Network Freedom' principles, 2004.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle framed as a consumer entitlement to access lawful Internet content; used as normative basis for non-discrimination expectations from ISPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to run applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers should be able to run applications of their choice. (Powell, 2004.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports prohibition on ISPs blocking or restricting user-chosen applications (subject to other lawful restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to attach devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers should be permitted to attach any devices they choose to the connection in their homes. (Powell, 2004.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underpins policies preventing ISPs from refusing connection of non-harmful consumer devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to obtain service plan information
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers should receive meaningful information regarding their service plans. (Powell, 2004.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms the basis for transparency requirements obliging ISPs to disclose performance characteristics and network management practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumers' right to access lawful Internet content
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers are entitled to access the lawful Internet content of their choice. (FCC Internet Policy Statement / modified principles, 2005.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often cited as a core net neutrality requirement; grounds for 'no-blocking' rules and for legal challenges when ISPs restrict lawful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumers' right to run applications subject to law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers are entitled to run applications and services of their choice, subject to the needs of law enforcement. (FCC modified principles, 2005.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges limits where law enforcement needs or other legal obligations justify restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to connect legal devices that don't harm the network
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers are entitled to connect their choice of legal devices that do not harm the network. (FCC modified principles, 2005.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits ISPs to deny or restrict devices that would damage the network while protecting consumer attachment rights for lawful, non-harmful devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to competition among providers and content/services
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers are entitled to competition among network providers, application and service providers, and content providers. (FCC modified principles, 2005.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames net neutrality as also a competition policy concern; supports rules preventing ISPs from privileging certain providers to the detriment of competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open applications (Google 700 MHz condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers should be able to download and use any software application, content, or services they desire. (Google's 700 MHz auction conditions, 2008.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted in variant by FCC policy statements; used as a specific auction/license condition to preserve application openness on particular spectrum blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open devices (Google 700 MHz condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers should be able to use a handheld communications device with whatever wireless network they prefer. (Google's 700 MHz conditions, 2008.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a license condition to prevent device-locking and to encourage device/network interoperability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open services / wholesale access (Google 700 MHz condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties (resellers) should be able to acquire wireless services from a licensee on a wholesale basis, based on reasonably nondiscriminatory commercial terms. (Google's 700 MHz conditions, 2008.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aimed at ensuring wholesale access and preventing vertical foreclosure by licensees; used as a concrete market-structure condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open networks / interconnection (Google 700 MHz condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties, such as Internet service providers, should be able to interconnect at any technically feasible point in a licensee's wireless network. (Google's 700 MHz conditions, 2008.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeks to preserve technical interconnection rights to promote competition and openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers and innovators have a right to know the basic performance characteristics of their Internet access and how their network is being managed. (One of the 2010 FCC Open Internet Order principles.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires ISPs to disclose network management practices, performance metrics, and terms of service; in practice led to obligations to publish such information and to disclose changes and compliance plans (e.g., Comcast order).

rubrics_metrics.name: No blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Right to send and receive lawful traffic; prohibits the blocking of lawful content, apps, services and the connection of non-harmful devices to the network. (2010 Open Internet Order principle.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a direct prohibition on ISP actions that prevent users from accessing lawful Internet resources; central to net neutrality enforcement and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level playing field / no unreasonable discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers and innovators have a right to a level playing field; ban on unreasonable content discrimination and no approval for 'pay for priority' arrangements (fast lanes). (2010 Open Internet Order principle.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibits ISPs from giving preferential treatment that disadvantages other content providers; explicitly targets paid-prioritization schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network management (reasonable network management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance for broadband providers to engage in reasonable network management; rules do not forbid providers from offering subscribers tiers of services or charging based on bandwidth consumed. (2010 Open Internet Order principle.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits technical measures for congestion, security, or other network needs so long as management is 'reasonable' — a contested standard in enforcement and litigation; distinguishes permissible management from discriminatory practices like paid prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile-specific application of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Net neutrality provisions do not apply as strongly to mobile devices; some provisions (transparency and no blocking) still apply to mobile broadband providers. (2010 Open Internet Order principle.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes technical and market differences in mobile networks and tailors the scope of certain obligations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigilance / monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an open Internet advisory committee to assist the commission in monitoring the state of Internet openness and the effects of the rules. (2010 Open Internet Order principle.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional mechanism for ongoing oversight, evidence gathering, and potential rule adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title II reclassification (common carrier treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reclassify Internet service providers as Title II common carrier telecommunication services to treat broadband as a public good and to allow the FCC to impose common-carrier obligations (2015 Open Internet Order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal mechanism to bring strong non-discrimination authority (e.g., subsection 202(a)) to bear on ISPs; in practice corresponded to fuller enforceability of no-blocking, no-throttling, and no-paid-prioritization rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 706 statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Section 706 of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 as a statutory basis to regulate broadband providers to 'promote deployment' and to promulgate rules governing broadband providers’ treatment of Internet traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FCC has relied on Section 706 to justify certain rules while courts have disputed whether Section 706 alone supports stringent non‑discrimination rules when ISPs are classified under Title I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsection 202(a) unjust or unreasonable discrimination standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Title II common-carrier law (subsection 202(a)), common carriers cannot 'make any unjust or unreasonable discrimination in charges, practices, classifications, regulations, facilities, or services.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a statutory standard for prohibiting discriminatory practices; central to arguments in favor of Title II reclassification to obtain enforceable anti-discrimination authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and compliance obligations as enforcement tools
rubrics_metrics.description: FCC can require ISPs to disclose network management practices, submit compliance plans, and publicly report intended practices (as in the Comcast orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical enforcement mechanism that accompanied findings of wrongdoing: public disclosure and formal compliance plans used to remediate problematic ISP behavior even where fines were not imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization in state laws and proposed bills
rubrics_metrics.description: State-level legislative proposals and enacted laws commonly prohibit ISPs from blocking, throttling, or otherwise unreasonably disadvantaging consumers, and ban paid prioritization. (Multiple state bill examples cited.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of federal Title II mandates, states have adopted their own net neutrality protections; rules vary but often mirror the core 'no blocking / no throttling / no paid prioritization' framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: License/auction-specific openness conditions and selective application
rubrics_metrics.description: When auctioning spectrum or issuing licenses, the FCC may (and has) impose(d) openness conditions (e.g., open applications/devices) on particular blocks and can apply or withhold such conditions selectively. (Example: Google 700 MHz bid and FCC adoption of two of four conditions.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows an administrative, contract-based tool for promoting openness on discrete resources; illustrates that openness can be implemented via license terms rather than broad statutory classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions for pre-existing stronger state laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal rulemaking (e.g., 2015 order) may make exemptions for states that have already established stronger net neutrality protections. (2015 FCC made exemptions for North Carolina and Tennessee.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges federal-state interactions and the possibility of preserving state-level protections when federal rules are adopted with carve-outs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness / 'good reason' standard for network restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory and enforcement statements invoke a 'good reason' or 'reasonable' standard to justify when ISPs may limit access or manage networks (e.g., Kevin Martin's statement that operators can't prevent access 'unless there is a good reason').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This amorphous standard appears in enforcement discussions and is a locus for dispute: what constitutes a 'good reason' for blocking or throttling is contested and often litigated.
